content: Your doctor has prescribed antihemophilic factor (recombinant) to assist your blood in clotting. This medication will be administered either directly into your vein or through an intravenous fluid that drips via a needle or catheter placed in your vein. The infusion typically lasts about 5 to 10 minutes. Depending on your condition, it may be given as frequently as two to three times daily or as infrequently as once every two or more weeks. Antihemophilic factor (recombinant) is a synthetic version of substances naturally produced by the body. It works by activating clotting factors in your blood to form clots and reduce bleeding episodes. In some cases, this medication may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider (doctor, nurse, or pharmacist) may monitor the effectiveness and potential side effects of your treatment through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting antihemophilic factor (recombinant), inform your doctor and pharmacist if you have ever had a reaction to this medication or if you are allergic to any drugs. Additionally, disclose if you are taking any medications such as prednisone, cyclophosphamide (Cytoxan), cyclosporine (Neoral, Sandimmune), heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin (Lovenox, Normiflo), interferon alfa (Roferon-A, Intron), vincristine (Oncovin), vitamin K, or other vitamins. Notify your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. If you become pregnant while taking this medication, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform your doctor or dentist that you are taking antihemophilic factor (recombinant) before any procedures. Before administering antihemophilic factor (recombinant), carefully inspect the solution. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or examine the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Use a new solution, but show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your medication instructions precisely. Do not stop your therapy for any reason without consulting your healthcare provider. Do not alter your dosing schedule without discussing it with your healthcare provider. If you experience a mechanical problem, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop the infusion. If this occurs, contact your healthcare provider immediately to resume your therapy. Antihemophilic factor (recombinant) may cause side effects. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they are severe or persistent: dizziness, headache, sore throat, itching, upset stomach, vomiting, or fatigue. If you experience any of the following symptoms, stop the infusion and contact your healthcare provider immediately: increased pulse rate, hives, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, chest discomfort or tightness, chills, or fever. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Your healthcare provider will likely provide you with a supply of antihemophilic factor (recombinant) for several days at a time and will instruct you on how to prepare each dose. Store your medication as directed, and ensure you understand the proper storage requirements. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and store all medications and supplies out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will also instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call 911 or your local emergency services immediately. If you are receiving antihemophilic factor (recombinant) through a vein or under your skin, it is important to recognize the symptoms of a catheter-related infection, which is an infection at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin.
